utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will be -- I'll be fairly brief, Your Honour. Your Honour already kind of covered one of the topics, and that was Ms. Korner's assertion that we had ten days or so to sit in July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. That's I think superseded now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Actually, I looked at the last four months, and I may be off a day or two but 16 days in July is -- is a little above average for what we've been able to do so far, so I don't think it's -- I think that's about all we can hope for in any month is 16 or 17 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you if you don't mind me interrupting you that basically I have studied this very carefully, a comparative study. I mean, each court -- each Trial Chamber in each case basically sits for 15 -- 15 or 16 times in a month. That's not an average; it's standard. So that's what we are talking about. In July, that's what we have. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other things I just would like to respond somewhat briefly to some things that Ms. Korner said yesterday afternoon. And I do that recognising her statement this afternoon regarding that. The two things that I would like to focus on - and I will do it briefly, Your Honours - is first of all her suggestion that we're not contesting some things. It's my understanding -- and if -- if I'm wrong, I should be told I'm wrong. It's my understanding that by entering a plea of not guilty a defendant puts in contest every allegation of the indictment filed against him by the Prosecutor and puts the Prosecutor to the burden of proving each and every allegation in that indictment beyond a reasonable doubt. One does not have to keep saying day after day, "We contest this indictment. We contest this indictment. We contest this indictment." The plea of not guilty does that. What has happened since that plea of not guilty is that in some very limited instances we have told Ms. Korner some things that we do not contest. And I want to emphasise that what we've told her are things we do not contest. And we've had a discussion about this Your Honour will remember, when I said it will make it easier for us to deal with some of these matters if we could take a position of not contesting them rather than a position of admitting them. And for instance, with some of the killings, it would be impossible for us to admit them because we couldn't possibly now, but we can certainly say we don't contest them, which is what we've done. So the proposition that we're not contesting things just isn't so. We're contesting this indictment. We're putting the Prosecutor to her burden of proving the guilt of my client, at least, beyond a reasonable doubt. The other thing that I would take extraordinarily strong issue with is this: I don't know of a court anywhere in the world - there might be one, but if there is I don't know about it - where the Prosecutor can say to the judges, "I will put on witnesses until you tell me I have proved my case and then I'll go on to the next issue." That's not the way it works. It is the job of the Prosecutor to present whatever evidence it is she believes is sufficient to prove her case beyond a reasonable doubt, and she is not entitled to enlist the assistance of the Court in telling her when she has done that. She can only find out whether she's done that or not at the end of the case when the Court enters its judgement. Now, it's entirely appropriate, however, and it's done rather frequently in this Tribunal for the Court to say, "With regard to this issue, we believe four witnesses will be sufficient. Pick your best four."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I think that's what Ms. Korner meant.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I read Ms. Korner, how I understood her; not as you put it in the beginning. I mean, she was inviting the Tribunal to -- the Chamber to tell -- to tell her if you think we should curtail the evidence on, for example -- I don't know. I mean, it's -- the hygiene conditions or the conditions generally in Manjaca. Stop us -- say no more witnesses, we don't want any more witnesses on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's exactly my point. That is improper. It's entirely proper for you before Manjaca or before Sanski Most or before any issue that the Prosecutor is going to go into to say, "We think you should only put on four witnesses about this, so pick your best four."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What did I tell her yesterday? I told her we can only tell you -- we can -- limit yourself to the five best witnesses that you think you have. And that's her choice, not ours definitely. She knows exactly who the five or six or seven would be. But let's -- let's talk the only language that we four understand here. Okay? In other words -- we three understand. The Defence, the Prosecution, and us, the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know as much as I do and we do that with each and every new witness that is brought forward by the Prosecution, evidence may result as a consequence which strengthens the case of the Prosecution or it may well be the case that upon cross-examination, you will score one or two or three or four if not more hits, which you wouldn't have scored if that witness hasn't been brought over. And this is something that anyone trained to be a prosecutor knows and anyone who has been trained to be a Defence counsel knows. The same applies to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will not comment on the cross-examinations that have been taking place here, because I -- as a Judge and as an ex-Defence counsel, I have my own opinion on how I would have conducted cross-examination with each and every particular witness that we've had here. But I am not going to teach you anything, either Madam Fauveau or yourself or the rest of the teams, of the risks involved in putting questions only to have a negative answer which will weaken your case and strengthen the Prosecution's case. And I don't need to elaborate on these things because these are techniques of advocacy and -- on either side that I'm pretty well sure they're -- that you're masters of. The thing is this: Don't expect this Trial Chamber as long as it is presided by me to interfere much on how many witnesses you want to bring forward to strengthen, in support of your case, be it the Defence or be it the Prosecution. I'm not going at any one time to tell you, "I think we've had enough witnesses on -- on the conditions in Manjaca or on the conditions in Omarska and other camps," -- if there have been other cases, please do remember that the Trial Chamber is authorised to apply one of the Rules and take judicial notice of what has been decided in other cases. And I'm not excluding that at one point in time we might resort to that, very limitedly but we might resort to that. But in the case of Manjaca, this is as far as I know the first case that has been dealing with -- with Manjaca. So the way I see it as a presiding trial Judge that the Prosecution has got a tremendous burden, because what results in this case may also be important in other cases that will come up later on. I'm not going to tell the Prosecution, "I'm fed up. I don't want to hear any more. I'm fed up that the -- the conditions of hygiene, food, whatever were absolutely horrific in Manjaca." Do you think I'm going to do that? But the Prosecution knows that the more witnesses it brings over here, the more it's exposing these witnesses to cross-examination. And the more of them come here -- I mean, if they are going to prove what is already abundantly clear, that's up to the Prosecution to decide at -- but I think in all fairness to Ms. Korner that as we have been going along, there have been decisions taken to cut it short and cut it short not because there has been any particular intervention from this Trial Chamber. You know that there hasn't. But I think I am -- we -- the three of us are particularly lucky in this -- in this trial to have a very high class level of advocacy. And more or less you know exactly where you are. I mean, you -- I am pretty much sure that the -- the two of you or the three of you know exactly what you're doing. So I didn't take Ms. Korner as inviting the Court yesterday to tell her, "Yes, we are pretty much satisfied now that you have proven to us that the conditions in Manjaca were absolutely hopeless." Let me mention one small point yesterday. The fact that this witness that we had yesterday told us that he was issuing death certificates which basically were a misrepresentation of the truth, of which he was pretty much aware did Madam Fauveau grasp that and try to turn it into her advantage? Of course she did. Would she have been able to do that had yesterday's witness not come forward to give evidence? She wouldn't have been able to do that. So this is our -- I mean, he was an essential witness obviously. I mean, he was one of the key witnesses in this municipality and as far as Manjaca is concerned. But these are -- these are the realities of any trial that I have lived and you have lived and that you will continue to live in this trial, and I don't need to explain much more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in complete agreement with everything you just said, and I appreciate what you just said. It was what I was actually trying to point out myself. And with that, I have nothing further to say. So thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And please don't take Ms. Korner -- I did not misunderstand Ms. Korner yesterday. She was quite fair, actually. She -- what I understood she was trying to do is to try and -- working on the assumption that we had only ten days in July, she was trying to see if we could find a way out in which to lessen the amount of witnesses. But that's up to you. I'm not going -- I will interfere only when there is either a relevance, complete irrelevance or when there is a super abundance or something that has not been contested. Yes, there may also be a time when I will intervene -- and this may be sooner than you think -- when I will stop either Ms. Korner -- be it Ms. Korner or yourself in certain delicate moments and I will take the witness in my hands. I have the intention of doing that precisely with one of the witnesses that's coming up pretty soon, if I see that the situation becomes dramatic or too delicate for any one of you to continue handle. That I have done in the past and I will do if necessary. But maybe I am anticipating things that might not happen, but I am preparing you for that. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I agree with everything that Mr. Ackerman said and I think that that also applies to General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nevertheless, there are certain things I would like to add, one of which concerns the evidence for the Defence and the other concerns my client and the indictment. As far as evidence is concerned, this Trial Chamber issued a directive relative to the admission of evidence. In this directive, the Trial Chamber decided that in this case, a rule which in English is called the Best Evidence Rule would be applied. I said in English because I don't think that in legal French language -- I don't think this rule exists in legal French language. Last week we had a witness who was in Manjaca, 7.29. This witness arrived in Manjaca at the end of August 1992, and we listened to the evidence that he presented for about two hours relating to the conditions in Manjaca between June and August 1992. It seems that this witness is not the one who could present the best evidence with regard to Manjaca. As far as the other issue is concerned - and this concerns my client - yesterday Mrs. Korner said -- it's on page 98 of the LiveNote -- [In English] "We allege that General Talic is directly responsible for not controlling the conditions in that camp." [Interpretation] It seems on the basis of this statement that the Prosecutor, Ms. Korner, considers General Talic responsible for not controlling what allegedly took place in the Manjaca camp. Not controlling doesn't enter the definition in the Statute 7(1) -- in article 7(1) of the Statute. Article 7(1) of the Statute provides for the planning, instigation to commit, ordering and the committing of crimes. The fact that someone didn't control this could enter into Article 7(3), and it relates to superior responsibility. But the indictment -- according to the indictment, General Talic is presumed responsible for what took place in Manjaca in a -- pursuant to Article 7(1) and pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute. If the Prosecutor considers that General Talic is responsible for what allegedly took place in the Manjaca camp, only on the basis of Article 7(3), then it's necessary for her to say so clearly and to modify the indictment with regard to the Manjaca camp. And this will certainly have an influence on the defence of General Talic the direction it takes, and will certainly contribute to the acceleration of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it needs a reply, because we have the indictment. But can I just say very quickly two words about what Mr. Ackerman has to say. The first is, a plea of not guilty means the indictment is contested. Of course it means that the responsibility of the accused for any of the events is under contest. It does not, we would submit, mean that -- that means that every single fact that is talked about in the indictment necessarily is contested. The second matter is this: And that goes back to -- and we still don't appear to have had a ruling from the Appeals Chamber. It goes back to the concept of putting one's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Are you aware of the decision of the Appeals Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There isn't one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The Appeals Chamber decided today -- I can -- I have it in French, because that's the only version that was made available. And this is the decision on your appeal on 90(H)(ii).

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Witness perhaps Your Honour would be kind enough to summarise it for counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The appeal has been rejected and our judgement has been confirmed. So the position is as it had been maintained by the Prosecution and by the Trial Chamber in its decision of -- so that is pretty much clear now -- even though when these last cross-examinations that we've had, more or less they have accepted to adopt what is required by --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. I mean, I've -- I've no complaint about that. And it's quite clear that if case has been put. With one exception -- and I'm only raising it because of what Mr. Ackerman says and because of what I said about Manjaca. Of course people's credibility in terms of whether they can say the gate was to the left or the hospital or death certificates has been tested. What has never been put in terms, and I understood it was because neither defendant was saying that they were in -- accused, I'm sorry, were saying they were in a position to know because neither had ever been to the camp what the conditions were like. But if the case for the Defence either through instructions or through other evidence that they're going to call or have is that when these witnesses say that there were constant beatings, that people died as a result of the beatings, that is not what happened. These witnesses have invented that or, as one can put it, over-egged the pudding, made it out to be much worse than it actually was -- then that is something that ought to be put to the witnesses in turn. Because Your Honours are entitled to see what their response is to a suggestion that they are either lying or about what they say happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, Ms. Korner. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that's my -- that's my only issue. Now, the reason I said no issue and I accept that I was rather overstating it, because clearly issues have been raised, is that no witness has so far -- it's been put to any witness that we've called about Manjaca that the beatings that talked about didn't take place. And that was my concern, and that is why I raised the question of whether it was necessary to call further evidence on that issue -- that part of the case which didn't -- hadn't been directly challenged. So that's the only reason I raised that. And Your Honour is quite right -- obviously Your Honours can't say we believe every word. You haven't heard all the evidence. I was merely trying -- seeking an indication --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I didn't understand that you were --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, that's the only thing I say about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the thing is, Ms. Korner, again -- and I appeal to your well-known experience in this field -- that at a certain time you ought to be in a position to make an assessment of the arsenal that the Defence may have at its disposal. Now, let's -- let's talk of beatings. If you suspect that the Defence might later on be in a position or may later on be in a position to practically neutralise your case, because you have based your case only on the evidence of two or three witnesses -- you have to make the assessment at any given moment -- you have to make an assessment. And it could vary. It could -- I mean, because each witness that has been in Manjaca, I assume, can testify on beatings, can testify on food, can testify on the other general conditions. I mean, hygiene, torture, killings, presence of any of the accused. I don't know. But you are the one to make that assessment. So -- and it could well be that -- I can -- I can easily tell you, "Restrict the number of witnesses dealing with the conditions in Manjaca to not more than six." I can easily do that. But any particular witness can testify on other things related to Manjaca. At that point in time, what am I going to tell you? Don't bring that witness? Or deprive you from being in a position -- because then if I say five witnesses only or six witnesses only, I'm putting you in a position where you have to make some very difficult decisions. And unless it's something on which I would have no qualms with my conscience, if I were to restrict the number of witnesses -- and what I'm saying to you applies equally to the Defence. I will not do it. Irrespective of what happens in other Chambers, I'm presiding over this Chamber, and this Chamber will go on as the three of us will agree-- at any given moment where there is a superabundance of something, we will let you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say this straight away: No witness has been called purely to talk about Manjaca and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that. We know that. This is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But Your Honour -- Your Honour said Your Honour will have to make a decision as to work out whether the Defence are going to neutralise it. Well, Your Honour, the only way one can do that is by the cross-examination. And that's what I mean going back to there's been no cross-examination on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But then you are in a position to make an assessment. As we go on --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- we are evaluating the nature of each cross-examination that we have had and we come to our open conclusions, I mean temporary conclusions because the basic conclusions will arrive at the end of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But more or less if we are in a position to know, considering the cross-examinations that we have had what to expect from the Defence, I think you are in the same -- the same position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Only, Your Honour, if the Defence are following the rules that Your Honour laid down and not rules which are current in their own jurisdictions, and that is putting to the witness all matters that are not agreed to. And if that's what's been followed, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But the Defence have got the decision of the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So they will have to live with that decision whether they like it or not. I mean, I know Mr. Ackerman is accustomed to the situation prevailing in the US which does not recognise anything like we have in 90 -- it is -- it exists somewhere in the States. But over all it does not exist. But this is the reality and this is what we have to live.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, I think -- I'm grateful for Your Honour's assistance. And I've raised the point. And Mr. Ackerman has responded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I also do appreciate, Ms. Korner, that you are always in a different position than the Defence is, because you have the duty to disclose overall, even material which will eventually work against your case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's -- may I say so very right and proper, because we're not here to seek a conviction against all odds. We're here to present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- all evidence to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Defence is not in the same position. So I do appreciate that while the Defence may have -- the Defence usually has much more information on the case of the Prosecution beforehand, while the same cannot be said with regard to the Prosecution. I do appreciate that. But it's not something that the Tribunal or the Chamber is called upon to act.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because that's the law and that's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour clearly, as Your Honours rightly said, it's for us to make the hard decisions as to how much evidence to put on. And as the case proceeds, that's what we're going to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Can we proceed? Usher, please -- the witness has no protective measures. No. In the meantime, while we await this witness, Ms. Korner I have had almost a panic station forthcoming from one section of my legal staff that is tasked with giving us the complete scenario with regard to the Banja Luka municipality, that they can't finish that satisfactorily unless they have the exhibit numbers for the 92 -- Rule 92 statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, they can't finish it anyhow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because we haven't called all the witnesses yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 92 bis statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. There was only one, I think, 92 bis statement in the end, and the next exhibit number up on the Banja Luka section -- because we jumped -- is Prosecutor's Exhibit 548.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 548. Madam -- will you take note of that, Inneke, please, and pass it on. Okay. We'll check on that. There is one very minor thing that I wanted to raise before we address the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I take you back in time to about two months ago and even more when there was a motion from the Prosecution to take depositions for use at trial, referring to Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And one plus one, and then responses, et cetera. Do I take it -- do you agree with me that that is now moot?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It doesn't require any sort of ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can the Chamber take it that it has been withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the Chamber will not deal with that motion and the responses that were forthcoming from the Prosecution, because it's -- the motion is being taken as having been withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I suppose technically I mean -- do we have to withdraw it? I'd rather --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I leave the option open. If you want --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We don't require a ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can just -- you don't require a ruling.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd just like to leave it in case the situation ever arises again so it's on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if it's still in existence the Defence also must enter a declaration whether they require a ruling. You don't require a ruling. So since there's -- okay. Madam Fauveau also doesn't require a ruling. So there will be no ruling on that motion. Yes. Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am the Presiding Judge. And before I proceed any further, I think I ought to apologise to you for keeping you waiting for the past hour. The reason for this delay is not something capricious. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. It's because we had some procedural, legal matters to discuss and decide upon which were important. They do not relate to your evidence or your presence here, so you don't need to worry about them, because you had absolutely -- you have absolutely nothing to do with them. But I needed to apologise to you first and foremost for having kept you here waiting for one hour. I hope you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And I appreciate that very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Now, before you start giving evidence, the procedure here is that you enter a solemn declaration that you will tell us the truth in the course of your deposition. The gentleman standing by your side will give you a piece of paper on which there is a solemn declaration which I kindly invite you now to read out aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And -- yes. And now before we start with your questioning, may I just explain to you where you are and what's going to happen. As I told you, I am the Presiding Judge. I am flanked to my right -- at my right by Judge Janu from the Czech Republic. By the way, my name is Agius and I come from Malta. And on my left I have Judge Taya from Japan. We will be the three Judges that will be deciding -- we will be hearing the evidence in this trial and eventually coming to a decision. The three persons right in front of me are the members of the Registry. And to your right -- you don't need to worry about the persons in the back. They are my legal staff -- our legal staff. And the three persons in the front are the team for the Prosecution. And you are going to be examined by the lady in the middle, Madam Richterova. When the examination-in-chief of the Prosecution is terminated, then you will be examined by two Defence teams. The first team is to your left, front row, the first three persons. You will be examined -- cross-examined by one of them - I don't know who - but you will be examined by one of them. And the first team represents -- is the Defence for -- is in charge of the Defence of Radoslav Brdjanin, one of the accused in this trial. The other accused is General Talic, and he will be represented by Madam Fauveau, who is the lady at the extreme end of the front row. She will be the one to cross-examine you on behalf of General Talic. Having said that, if you have any questions, any queries, you can put them to this Chamber and we'll try to do our best to answer them. If you don't, we can proceed with the series of questions that the Prosecution will be making, putting to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Please can you state your full name for the record and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: My name is Grgo Stojic. I was born on the 30th of January, 1968.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I'm a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you are of the Catholic faith; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you were born in the village of Skrljevita in the Sanski Most municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, how many times did you give a statement in respect of the events which occurred during the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, I gave statements five times.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: As far as my memory serves me, I think that I made five statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can -- do you remember giving a statement in -- to the court in Sanski Most in 1996?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know who took the statement in that court?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I do. The municipal judge in Sanski Most, Mr. Adil Draganovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was this statement typed or recorded in some other way?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: First it was recorded and then typed out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And when did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: The next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was it in the presence of the Judge Draganovic?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you see Judge Draganovic to sign it at the same time?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, you were born in the village of Skrljevita. What was the ethnic composition of this village?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: The majority population were of Croat ethnicity, and there was a smaller percentage of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher to show the witness the Exhibit P757.2. It is the map of Sanski Most which has already been exhibited. Can you please place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you assist the Judges and show on the map the village of Skrljevita, please.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether there were other Croat villages in the municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you show us these villages and can you name them.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I can. The village of Sasina, the village of Poljak. It is the suburbs of Sanski Most. A part of Gornji Kruhari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, sir. Stop. Madam Richterova, the document itself, top left, indicates the villages which are predominantly Croat, Muslim, or Serb. So the proper question to put is sir, look at the towns or villages shown in red. Would you agree that these were predominantly Croat. And we'll leave it at that. That would cover the entire question without the need of the witness having to go through his memory to tell us whether -- which village and -- if he disagrees with that, he will obviously tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Would you please answer the question which was posed by the Judge Agius, whether it is correct that these villages marked in red are predominantly occupied by Croats.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojic, you served your compulsory military service from December 1990 till January 1992. Did you return -- from the military service, did you return back to your village?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After you returned to your village, were you able to observe any differences in how Serbs treated Croats in comparison with Muslims?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I noticed that already since the multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, ever since 1990. And then after returning from my military service, as I was passing -- going from Sarajevo to Sanski Most, from Mrkonjic Grad towards Kljuc, we were stopped by a patrol, a patrol of the military police. They entered the bus to check things out, and then we set off Sanski Most. The war in Croatia had already started at the time, that is, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, I would like you to focus on the year 1992. And briefly if you could state in which way, if ever, the life was different from the years before.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: The referendum was already in the offing, and it was indeed held on the 29th of February and the 1st of March, 1992. Only the Croats and Muslims took part in the referendum. But let me go back to the year 1990 and the multi-party elections. In the voting station in Skrljevita, where I lived, the Serbs from a part of Skrljevita did not vote at that polling station and they tore down posters of the Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ, so that after returning from the front in Croatia, the Serbs who went to Croatia on a voluntary basis, they would pass through the village shooting, throwing grenades. Also a plane would fly at very high speed and through the sound barrier so that the people were already in a lot of fear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we now go to the year 1992, and can you briefly state whether there were any restrictions on movement in your area, as far as you are aware.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Until the 19th of April, 1992 there were no restrictions on movement. But when the first attack occurred against Sanski Most municipality, which was carried out on the 26th and the 27th and 28th of May 1992, freedom of movement was restricted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us in which way.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, we weren't able to get through to Sanski Most because of the radio, the Serbian radio in Sanski Most. They called for weapons to be surrendered, weapons which we did not have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will deal with this announcement in respect of surrender of weapons. But I would like to go back to this freedom of movement. Did you see any checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I was going to Sanski Most, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who managed these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: There were Serbs who were armed and wearing civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were they all in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Those who weren't in civilian clothing, what did they wear?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: They were wearing military camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did they belong to any military unit, to your awareness?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I know that part of them belonged to the reserve forces of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When we are talking about these checkpoints, what was the purpose of these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: The purpose of the checkpoints was to control, to control -- to check who was going to town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before you said that you weren't able to freely move. What if you wanted to go from one place to another? Did you need to have any permission?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't go to such places; a friend of mine did, Franjo Ilicevic. He went to his relatives in the village of Kljevci. He had to obtain a pass in order to go there, allowing him to move.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did he tell you from whom he obtained this permission?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: He obtained it from the police station in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was it normal procedure that if you wanted to move to other places within the municipality, you had to have a permission?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: In a situation of war, yes, this is normal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I will move to surrender of weapons. Did you hear any announcement -- announcements in respect to surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where did you hear it?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Over the Serbian radio Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what was the announcement?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: The announcement was -- well, first of all, they listed all the Croat and Muslim villages in the area of the municipality of Sanski Most, and they were ordered to surrender all their weapons which were in their possession.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you remember that specifically Muslims and Croats were mentioned?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What else was stated in this announcement?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: It said that weapons should be collected at a certain point, at a certain spot, that the vehicles should be marked with a white flag and should go to the Crisis Staff in Sanski Most. That's where the headquarters of the Serbian armed forces were located.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were there any weapons in your village?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: There were some for hunting. There were a few pistols, and people had permits for these.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you hand them over?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know Ivica Tutic?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who is -- or who was Ivica Tutic?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: He was someone from my village. He was a capable man. He was capable for work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was he involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was he the person who took the weapons who were surrendered in your village?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. We surrendered them to him because this is what he was ordered to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Ivica Tutic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: At the beginning -- in the beginning of July, Ivica was ordered to report to the Sanski Most police station. The policemen went to his home. He wasn't at home in the morning. He was ordered to report by 9.00 in the morning to the Sanski Most police station, which is what he did. And after that point in time, his trace got lost.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, you told us that you heard announcement to surrender weapons.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you hear any speeches on the radio made by Muslims during the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did hear speeches. The dentist Fajko Biscevic was brought in and Dr. Enes Sabanovic. That's what the speaker said on the radio. He said, "Now you will be addressed by the leaders." And they did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you remember what their speech -- what their speeches were about?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I do remember. Using those words, they were literally asking the Croats and Muslims to surrender their weapons, the weapons that they had in their possession and said that in this way peace and security would be guaranteed for them. Whoever wanted to leave would be enabled to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned that in this speech was said that if people want to leave the municipality, they were allowed to do it. Did you hear this similar speeches from other sources about the movement of people out of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I did hear things from other people -- from people. Your Honours, I would like to return to the meeting which was held in Kruhari in the course of the attack on Sanski Most. When Ilija Tutic was called, Bono Tutic and Ivica Tutic, when these men were called. And on the Serbian side, Delic Tomo was present and another military officer. And on the following day, we were told in the village by Bono Tutic, we were told about what had been agreed, about what Mr. Delic had told them, what he said we had to do. He told us that we had to surrender 86 rifles, which we had allegedly obtained from Croatia. Mesic and Tudjman had allegedly sent them to us. Delic literally told Bono and the others that he had done this because we were friends and that there would be no further discussion that weapons had started talking. Then he said, "Gather what weapons there are." And Ivica Tutic, whom I have mentioned, took them away, as I have already said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, can I go back to my previous question about announcements or speeches made in relation of moving people out of the municipality. Have you heard any such speeches?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear such speeches.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I can. There was announcement over the Serbian radio in Sanski Most, and it said, "Everyone who wants to leave the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most must come to the -- to an office to room 26 in the municipality building and those who so wish will be allowed to leave." And also those who wanted to leave were allegedly guaranteed -- those who wanted to stay were allegedly guaranteed peace and security in the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most. Those who wanted to do so had to submit a request for a permanent permit of residence. Some people did this and Bono Tutic was among them. He received this permit. And rumour has it that whoever received such a permit if someone checked his papers when he would show his papers that person checking the papers wouldn't be able to do anything to him, wouldn't harm him in any way. And basically this was a sort of identity card showing you weren't a Serb. And this is like what the Nazis did to the Jews.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, I will return again to the question about the movement of people outside. You mentioned that who wanted to move had to apply for a permission. Have you heard any speech or statement stating how many people would be allowed to stay?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear anything. But people said - Serbs, friends, neighbours - that only 2 per cent would remain.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you say "only 2 per cent would remain," do you mean in the municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: May I only show the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: -- one paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please do. And then we'll break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And this exhibit, which was premarked P811. On the bottom, there is a Prosecution exhibit number. P811. Can we place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned that whoever wanted to leave had to apply for the permission. Can you have a look at the document next to you and tell us whether this is the permission for leaving the municipality.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was it issued -- to whom this permission was issued?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: It was issued to myself, to my mother, and to my brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And we can see the date 21st of September, 1992, but we know that you stayed in that municipality much longer. Why didn't you leave after you obtained this permission?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, we weren't able to, because there were no convoys at the time and individual people were already getting ready in my village for a convoy. They were getting ready to leave. But they didn't manage to do so either. When I went to get this certificate, my sister and I went to the Sanski Most municipal building. We went to room 26, and we asked to move. The gentleman who was in that office told us to contact our representative who was organising the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you do it?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did they manage to arrange something for you?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think we will break now -- we can break now and I will start the new subject after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Richterova. We will break. I understand you require 20 minutes. So we'll break for 20 minutes starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, now I want to direct you back to your village, and I want you to tell the Court what happened on 2nd November of 1992. Is it correct that on the 2nd of November in the morning you left for Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: With whom did you go?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I went with my aunt's son, my aunt -- who was called Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was her son's name?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: His name was Dragan Tadic. I went with my aunt's son who was called Dragan, the son.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You stayed till midday and then you were -- you set out for your village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: On your way back to Skrljevita, did you meet any of your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Whom did you meet?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Ante Tutic, Petar Nikic, Zarko Nikic, and Josip Banovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you go together or did these people went ahead of you?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Dragan and I went together.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And these four men?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: They went ahead of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were on the way to Skrljevita. Can you tell the Court what happened on the way.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of the Glamosnica forest, which leads towards Skrljevita, we fell into an ambush. Behind bushes by the road there were people in uniform and in civilian clothing with machine-guns, light machine-guns. We said good day to them. They didn't reply. They asked us where we were from. We said nothing. Then they asked us whether we had any papers on us, any form of identification. We said that we did. I first gave them my identity card. He took it and had a look at it and then returned it to me. Then Dragan gave his. He read his name out aloud and he used these words, "Tadic Nikola Dragan from Skrljevita," and he returned it to him. He then said, "We will join our men from the village. There are others."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will stop you here, Mr. Stojic. Can you describe these two men who stopped you?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: The first one was wearing civilian clothes. He had a short -- he was wearing a short leather jacket. He was of medium height. He had a thin beard, and he was carrying a light machine-gun which he supported against his leg. And on the butt there was a Serbian mark that was inscribed, four S's. The second man was next to him. He was in uniform. He was wearing a camouflage uniform. He had a beret on his -- he was wearing a beret, and there was a cockade on the beret and a Serbian cross next to it. He had the belt belonging to the military police. It was a white belt. He had handcuffs on him, a truncheon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you know these two men from before?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't know them personally, but I had seen them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you know their name at the time?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you learn their names at a later point?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I found it out from my friends, who knew them personally. The man in civilian clothes, his name was Danilusko Kajtez, known as Dane. He was also well known as a Chetnik. The second man was Zoran Vukojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you learned these names from your friends; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: These two men asked you to join them -- and I will correct myself. They asked you to follow them and join your neighbours or the other people who were further in the forest; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you join them?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who were these men?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: When we arrived there -- when we got there from the road, behind the bushes by the river itself, as soon as we arrived there I saw on a sand -- a pile of sand, someone with a light machine-gun in uniform. He was pointing it at the four men and these men were Ante Tutic, Zarko Nikic, Petar Nikic, and Josip Banovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What happened after you joined these men?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: They then lined us up. They ordered us to raise our hands and then turn to the left. When we turned around, they said, "Put your hands down. It will be easier for you to hold on." And then we were searched. There was another man behind the bushes in uniform. He wasn't very tall, fairly well built. He had curly brown hair. He also joined in the search. But he didn't actually carry out the search.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you describe this uniform. Can you be more precise.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: The uniforms were also military camouflage uniforms, only they had nothing on their heads. Light machine-guns were the same, and also the four S's were carved onto the rifle butts. All of them had two clips of ammunition each.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After they finished the search, what followed?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: They then started questioning us, where we were keeping guard duty, where we slept, where our leader was, the leader of the HDZ. "Where is Ilija Tutic," they said. "Where is Bono Tutic?" All of us were put questions of this kind. And while they were searching us, they seized all our personal documents, the money we had on us, our personal belongings. They called out Zare and Pero by their names. And from that, one can infer that they knew them well. When Dragan and I arrived there, Zare cried out, "My poor children," and Pero started sobbing. We were all hit on the shoulders with truncheons, and then we were ordered to get closer to one another. When the finished the search, they said, "We are Seselj army. Then they moved away and I heard the command start. Then the shooting started. There was the one with his light machine-gun pointed at us, and we had our backs turned to him, so that I wasn't able to see who actually committed the murder. I thought to myself Dear God, will anyone survive to tell others what happened. When similar killings occurred, if the Muslims were the victims then they said it was the Ustashas that had killed them. If Croats were killed, they said it was the Green Berets that had killed them. When executions took place by firing squad, when this execution took place I got a bullet in my left upper arm and I fell straight to the ground. As I was lying there on the ground, I felt I had -- that a bullet had hit my hip and that the exit wound was through my stomach. So I stayed there for a while lying down. When they had finished this execution, I heard them saying, "Let's run for it." And I could hear them running and the sound that their weapons made. I lay there for a minute or two; I don't remember exactly for how long. Then I raised my head and turned left and right and then returned my head to the ground, lay my head on the ground again, listening to make sure that they were not somewhere nearby. Then I got up. And when I got up, my hand was quite numb. The blood was flowing. Also I had an entry and exit wound in my stomach. I just felt my fingers. Then I put my hand in my jacket. I turned around and what I saw was a horrific scene. Banovic Josip, Zarko Nikic, Ante Tutic, and Petar Nikic had fallen towards this rivulet. On top of those bodies were Zarko Nikic, whom I could see well. I could see well what he looked like. His skull had been blown to bits. Blood was flowing. They were touching the water of the river. The brain was seeping out and the blood was mixing with the water. Dragan Tadic fell a metre or two away from me. He was curled up somehow, and he was on the ground, on the grass. I saw that no one was crying for help, and I saw that these men had been shot dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where did you go after you observed the death of your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: After that I moved away from the scene of the crime and headed towards the river. I covered some 30 metres from the crime scene and then I continued through the water. So I reached a meadow that used to be owned by the late Zarko Nikic at the foot of the Glamosnica wood. I crossed this meadow and went into the wood slowly, but then the pain got worse so that I could only move slowly, taking rests every so often.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. You were -- where were you heading?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: In the direction of Skrljevita.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: On the way to Skrljevita, at any point did you hear a sound of fire, bursts of fire?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I was in the woods, I first heard the sound of a tractor and I thought to myself that they were looking for me. However, there was a small stream there running through the wood itself and some branches, so I hid there. Then I heard again at the bottom of the wood the sound of very strong bursts of fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you learn at some later stage what happened?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did learn what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What did you learn?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I learnt when I was in Banja Luka ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What did you learn when you were in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: My sister came to see me at the ward where I was being treated. No, I'm sorry, not my sister. Ivo Tutic's sister; who was killed but not at the same time when I was shot. She heard about me, that I was in Banja Luka, and she approached me and greeted me and she said that her brother had been killed as well as Bruno Tutic, Adlo Tatic [phoen], and Josip Fertalac [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I interrupted you. When you described your way towards the Skrljevita and then you heard the burst of fire. Can you now describe further the way to the Skrljevita. Did you manage to get some help on your way?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I can. First of all, badly injured as I was, I managed to somehow reach the house of Zarko Nikic, who had been killed. In front of the house, the dogs started barking and his children came out. When they saw the condition I was in, they asked about their father and started crying. Just then I told them to keep quiet because they could come and kill them as well. I said that Zare had been killed, but they didn't believe me. So I entered the house. His daughter led me in. And I sat down for a while inside. They started asking me questions again. I told them then that I didn't know that he had been killed, because I was afraid that the screaming might attract them and they might come and kill them as well. They ran off then to the house of the -- of Pero Nikic -- Petar Nikic, who had also been killed, and his wife was there. His wife's name and Marija, Marija Banovic, the mother, whose son Josip had been killed. Then Zarko's daughter came back. She gave me a hand. And as we were leaving the village, or the hamlet called Numara, Pero's wife and the mother of Josip, both of whom had been killed, arrived together with two small children who were underage. Zarko's wife had a small baby. I don't remember exactly how old the baby was. They left me there and they went on to the village looking for aid. However, I couldn't wait, so I slowly dragged myself to Joso Tutic's house. No one came, so slowly I started off towards the house of Josip Banovic, who had also been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, is it correct to say that at the end you managed to reach your village, you were -- first aid was given to you, and then you were taken on the cart to the health centre in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes. When I reached the house, I couldn't move any more. I was given first aid by Ante Ilicic, Josip Banovic's neighbour and my friend. Then all the locals by then had learnt of what had happened and my brother arrived with a horse-drawn cart and my neighbour Franjo Ilicic. Quite a large group of people had gathered by then. They carried me out of the house and laid me down in the cart. As we went forward with my brother and neighbour Franjo, my aunt's son Drago came as well. When we reached the hamlet of Tutici, there was a large crowd of people there. When they saw me, Josip Ptalec's wife and Bono Tutic's wife said that there was no Bono and no Tomica. I replied, "Who hadn't come, wouldn't come," because there was no chance of them getting through.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, you were -- as you agreed, you were taken on the cart to Sanski Most, where you were provided with first aid in the health centre. And then from Sanski Most, you were transferred to Prijedor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: From Prijedor, you were transferred to Banja Luka hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In Banja Luka hospital, what kind of treatment did you receive? Now I am talking about medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: When I arrived there, I was taken in on a stretcher. And in the admissions office, the nurse asked me which military unit I belonged to. I answered that I was not in the army, that I had been shot as a civilian, and they immediately prepared me for surgery. I woke up the next morning in the intensive care unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did you stay in this intensive unit?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Two days, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During your stay in Banja Luka hospital, were you transferred in some other unit within the hospital?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: On the 9th of November, I was transferred to the urology ward. But on the 9th already, the 9th of November, in the surgery ward where I was lying an incident occurred, that I mentioned before. Ivo Tutic's sister, whose brother had been killed, she was working at the ward, below where a person from my village called Ivo Nikic was lying. As we exchanged greetings. And she left. Ivo Nikic came to see me. Next to me Milan Oljaca was lying in a bed next to me, whose left leg had been amputated. Even before Nikic and I managed to greet one another, he felt ill, he was unwell. And then Nurse Nada ran in and asked, "What is it, Milan?" And he answered that he had never felt worse in his life than since this Ustasha had arrived there. Then she turned to Nikic and said to him, "What are you doing here? Get out." And she cursed him. "Do you want me to throw you out of the window," she said. After that, he left. I tried to explain to this Milan that this was a man from my village, and his response was that he was an Ustasha 100 per cent, that he personally had captured him in Croatia on the front and that he had been exchanged and how could an Ustasha come back. And then he said to me that he could change his ID card, that he could change everything, but that he would still be an Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, based on this incident what happened? Was it this incident -- was it after this incident when you were transferred to another ward within the Banja Luka hospital?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is when I was transferred, after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: But first Nurse Nada came and said to me the following: "Stojic, you will not leave the hospital until the military police releases you. There's no point in your family looking for you through the International Red Cross."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So where were you exactly transferred?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: As I said, I was transferred to the urology ward, in cell number 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you say "cell," how do you know that it was a cell?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Because a soldier was standing there and the nurse who had taken me there asked where she should put me. And this soldier had the door handle in his hand. He had taken it out of the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you said a cell. Does it mean it was a prison cell?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In which prison?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: In the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said a prison cell in hospital. But which prison did you --

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: -- do you mean?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I received an official report from the International Committee of the Red Cross that the prison is Tunjice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were taken into a cell. Were you during the time where you were in the cell, were you charged with something?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Officially I never received any indictment. But let me first explain the situation in cell number 8. When this soldier opened the door, the nurse asked him, "Where shall I put him?" He responded, "Throw him on the ground." There were some other wounded people there already who had been brought there from Kotor Varos, a person who had got injured at the Manjaca camp, and they were Muslims. I found there already on the bed -- sitting on the bed Ivo Nikic, and then we were shut up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, can you just briefly describe the sanitary conditions in this cell -- or in cells in which you were kept.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: When I arrived at that cell, the sheets were bloodstained, stained with pus. There was a heavy smell from the -- from the excreter. The window was slightly opened, but when I arrived at that cell we were given lunch. We got our lunch. When the soldier opened the door, we were ordered to raise three fingers up like this. Then he said, "That's how you should do it. Now you are Serbs." Then these nurses came and they were shown how many Ustashas there were captured there. When we finished lunch, the soldier ordered the serving lady to count the forks, to make sure we didn't kill ourselves. And then we stayed for a certain time in that cell number 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you transferred to some other cell?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How many people were in the other cell?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: There were five.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us how were you treated during your stay in the cell. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Before my actual transfer, I was pushed into the corridor. Nurse Ljubisava was wearing a green hospital uniform. She started mistreating me there, harassing me. She asked me how many Serbs I had killed, how many Serb women I had raped, how many children I had slaughtered. Then she brought in a passer-by who stank of alcohol to see an Ustasha. And then he took it out on me. He started insulting me, and I tried to explain to him what I had been through, but it was all in vain. Where had I been captured. But there was no way I could explain it to him. When I explained how I had been wounded, he said, "What were you doing in the woods?" And then he went on to ask, "How many Serbs have you killed," again. When I tried to explain that I hadn't killed anyone, he said that I was lying. He asked Ljubisava to give him a bullet. Literally he said, "Give me a bullet so I can kill him." Then he said, "No, not a bullet. Give me a knife to cut his throat with. It's cheaper." Then they called a young boy of 12 or 13 who had his arm in a cast also to come and look at the Ustasha. I had a fixture on my left arm, and then this young boy said, "Look at the Ustasha. They've given him a fixture." So this went on for about half an hour. Then a soldier came. Again with the door handle in his hand and he opened cell number 9. I saw him do it. Then Nurse Ljubisava pushed me inside and said, "Choose whichever bed you want." I couldn't get up. I was on a trolley, and I had a drainage tube and I somehow managed to lie on the bed as you enter the room on the right-hand side of the window.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, how long did you stay in this cell? We understand you were transferred on 9 of November. How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: In cell number 8 or cell number 9?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The second cell.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: For a total of 32 days, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When were you released?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: I was released on the 11th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During the time you were in the cell number 9, these 32 days, how were you treated? Did you receive normal medical care?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: First of all, I was given an intravenous drip. The nurse brought in four or five bottles and put them on the table next to me. But the needle was stuck in a part of my arm where -- where the arm moves, so my vein burst and the intravenous drip dripped. There was a leak. When I asked for them to correct it she came and pulled it out. Then she gathered everything and took it away. But first of all, I should describe these others in cell number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, before you describe the others, I would really like you to answer my question about this medical treatment within these 32 hours -- sorry, within the 32 days. You said you were supposed to get this IV insulation, but you didn't receive it because the needle got stuck.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you receive the regular medical treatment in the time when you were in the cell?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: About this medical treatment. You were at the beginning complaining about the hygiene conditions. You said that the sheets were dirty. How often did they change these sheets?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, two or three times in all. And that was before delegates from the International Committee of the Red Cross came to visit. The 19th of November was the first time they visited. Then this cleaning lady came to tidy up the room. We realised -- we noticed that something would happen. A delegate from the International Red Cross came, and he was accompanied by a translator. As far as I can remember, I think his name was Sinisa [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So is it correct that your sheets were always changed in -- within -- before the visit of International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, can you tell the Court how you were treated by the guards and by the nurse -- by the nurses when you were in this cell. Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, very callously. They personally, and especially Nurse Ljubisava, would bring in wounded people from another ward to beat us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So were you beaten during the stay in the cell?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How many times were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Earlier on I said in my statement that they beat me on two occasions. But they did it on more occasions than that, because one didn't feel like counting at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What about the people who were with you in the cell? How were they treated?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Callously. I know that Ramiz Skoric who was killed in Manjaca -- who was wounded in Manjaca, he lost both legs. He said that Manjaca was great and that he was happy about the fact that we were going to be transferred to the Manjaca camp. So when they were taken away for questioning, that's what they were told.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, you said you were beaten more than one time. What about the people who were in the cell with you?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were they beaten?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. They beat everyone. While they were beating the people in cell number 8, we would hear terrible blows. We were -- we already started getting ready in cell number 9 in order to get through this more easily.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who did the beating?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: We were beaten by civilians and by soldiers and by anyone who could enter that cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you are referring to "soldiers," can you be more specific. What kind of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Serbian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you be even more specific. Were they regular reservists, military police?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Who knows what they were like. I think they were the ones who were sent away, who weren't under control. They were out of control.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic, what were the consequences of the event on the 2nd of November, 1992 for you?

utterances.speaker: GRGO STOJIC
utterances.text: Well, the consequences were terrible. I am permanently disabled. I'm not fit to work. And so to speak I'm not fit for life, for life which would be a dignified life for a man. But first of all, I should describe the conditions -- the other conditions in that notorious cell, especially the wounded who came in the evening, they would break their crutches when dealing blows to Ramiz Skoric. They used truncheons to beat us with. They would kick us. They would punch us. And I can remember when many of them entered the cell on one occasion, they maltreated us to such an extent -- they asked us for money. They took the gold that the Muslims had, their watches. They took everything. They also asked me to give them something, but I had nothing. On one occasion when they had beaten me, when he approached me he took the sheet off to see where I had been operated. He then covered me with the sheet again. Then he moved away and kicked me in the stomach. He continued kicking me until I started bleeding. And that's what happened with the others. That's what happened with the others too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojic. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can stop for a break. Would 15 minutes be okay now, or do you still require 20?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be happy with 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So it will be a 15-minute break. Strictly 15 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
